summary:
One More Sol is an interactive, browser-based Moon and Mars Habitat simulator that turns real NASA space data into hands-on survival decisions. Built with HTML5 canvas, JavaScript, and Three.js, the game lets players choose between Jezero Crater (Mars) and Shackleton Crater (Moon) and take on five specialized crew roles, from Mission Commander to Eva Specialist, to keep their ship or the outpost running for five sols. 

To address the challenge of making complex science accessible, the simulation integrates live Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) alerts from NASA's DONKI API alongside closed-loop life-support and astrobotany concepts from NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR). Instead of reading static datasets, players walk the ship, perform surface excursions, and navigate real engineering TRADE-OFFS: balancing battery power, oxygen scrubbing, magnetic radiation shielding, and crew medical treatment during solar storms. 

One More Sol matters because it bridges technical data with human storytelling, inspiring future explorers while reminding us that protecting fragile life-support systems is vital both in deep space and on Earth.
details:
One More Sol is an interactive, browser-based Moon and Mars habitat and Extravehicular Activity (EVA) simulator that turns real NASA space telemetry into human survival decisions. Instead of reading charts about deep-space hazards, players step inside a working lunar or Martian outpost and experience the real engineering trade-offs astronauts face across five sols (planetary days).

Players begin by selecting one of two authentic NASA exploration sites:
1. Jezero Crater, Mars - NASA's Perseverance landing site beside an ancient river delta, where Martian regolith dust accumulation steadily degrades solar panel efficiency.

2. Shackleton Crater, Moon - An Artemis target rich in permanently shadowed water ice, where extreme thermal swings drain battery reserves rapidly during long lunar nights.

Next, players choose from five real-world crew roles, each with distinct mission perks:
1. Mission Commander: Accelerates station-wide task execution by 20%.
2. Flight Engineer: Increases battery charging by 30% and reduces baseline power drain by 20%.
3. Mission Specialist: Amplifies OSDR biological research and closed-loop hydroponic crop output.
4. Flight Surgeon: Slows cumulative radiation buildup by 40% and boosts medical treatment efficiency.
5. EVA Specialist: Increases surface traversal speed by 15% and improves external sample collection.

Inspired by the spatial gameplay of Among Us and Soul Knight, players walk through their outpost and venture outside using keyboard controls (WASD/Arrow keys) or a responsive mobile virtual joystick. Approaching glowing terminals—the DONKI Power Node, OSDR Hydroponics Bioreactor, Magnetic Deflector, and Radiation Medbay—triggers interactive maintenance tasks. Every action involves a real physical trade-off: activating magnetic shielding protects the crew from solar flares, but drains electricity needed to scrub carbon dioxide from the air. Meanwhile, cumulative radiation exposure never resets on its own, requiring active shielding and Medbay treatment.

To ground gameplay in real space weather, the simulation queries NASA’s DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information) API for Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) events over the past 30 days to calibrate storm conditions, paired with an automatic offline simulation fallback and a one-click "Judge Demo" mode that jumps straight into an active solar storm.

One More Sol bridges the gap between complex planetary science and public imagination. By translating concepts like sols, coronal mass ejections, closed-loop life support, and cumulative radiation dosimetry into intuitive, high-stakes gameplay, our intended impact is twofold:

1. Inspiring Future Explorers: Students and everyday players experience astronauts not as distant heroes, but as collaborative problem-solvers managing fragile systems—sparking curiosity in STEM, heliophysics, and astrobotany.

2. Earth Stewardship: Managing scarce electricity, clean air, and water inside a sealed habitat mirrors our shared responsibility to protect finite life-support systems right here on Earth. Because the game runs instantly in any desktop or mobile browser with zero downloads, educators and science outreach programs can deploy it immediately.

On the technical side:
Core Languages & Web Standards: HTML5 Canvas (custom 2D top-down habitat renderer, procedural character engine, and animated starfield), Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), and CSS3.

NASA Open Data & Audio: NASA Open APIs (api.nasa.gov/DONKI/CME) for live solar storm telemetry, NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) concepts for life-support and astrobotany mechanics, and the native Web Audio API for procedural console alerts and sound effects.

Hardware & Workflow: Developed and cross-tested across standard student laptops and mobile smartphones to verify touch joystick ergonomics, frame-rate stability, and responsive screen scaling.

In terms of creativity we did the following:

Rather than building a passive data dashboard or a generic arcade shooter, we blended live heliophysics data with cozy, expressive character design and tactile spatial gameplay:

Custom Procedural "Astro-Chibi" Art Engine: Instead of relying on static image assets or simple color swaps, we programmed a vector-style Canvas rendering engine that draws distinct silhouettes and gear for every role—including a captain's cap for the Commander, safety goggles for the Engineer, a live astrobotany plant sprout growing on the Scientist's helmet, a medical headband for the Surgeon, and an animated cyan jetpack thruster with a caged visor for the EVA Specialist.

Data-as-Tension: Live CME telemetry isn't just displayed as text on the landing screen—it directly informs the urgency of balancing shields, power, and oxygen inside the base.

While creating the game we considered the following:
1. Scientific Authenticity vs. Playability: We incorporated real aerospace constraints (dust degradation on Mars, thermal battery drain at the lunar south pole, and non-resetting radiation dose) into 30-second sols and rapid minigames so players feel genuine mission pressure without needing an engineering degree.
2. Accessibility & Inclusivity: We built full keyboard navigation, support to skip background animations for motion-sensitive users, high-contrast HUD bars, and automatic mobile touch controls.
3. Resilience & Judge Experience: Knowing that live APIs can hit rate limits or offline environments during judging, we engineered an automatic offline storm fallback alongside a dedicated Judge Demo button so evaluators can test the core crisis loop in seconds.
